entries.q: What changes in GST from 1 November 2026?
entries.a: Following the 57th GST Council meeting in October 2026, CBIC issued Notification 03/2026-Central Tax, bringing sections 153 to 155 of the Finance Act, 2026 into force, and Notification 05/2026-Central Tax, the CGST (Amendment) Rules, 2026, both dated 26 October 2026. They apply from 1 November 2026, with some parts from 1 December 2026, 1 January 2027 and 1 April 2027. They cover quicker registration with fewer queries, faster refunds, refund of input tax credit on input services for businesses with an inverted duty structure, and registration of e-commerce sellers using the operator's warehouse. Draft versions of the redesigned GSTR-1, GSTR-1A and IFF forms were published for public comment until 30 November 2026. Changes that need further amendments to the GST Acts are expected from 1 April 2027; CBIC Instruction 02/2026-GST dated 30 October 2026 applies some of them to central GST officers in the meantime.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Will GST refunds now be paid faster?
entries.a: Yes, for most claims. Under rules 90 and 91 as amended by Notification 05/2026-Central Tax dated 26 October 2026, from 1 November 2026 the department must issue an acknowledgement or a deficiency memo within 10 days instead of 15, failing which the application is treated as acknowledged. For exports and other zero-rated supplies and inverted duty claims, 90% of the amount can be sanctioned provisionally through the portal on a risk-based check, within 3 working days of acknowledgement. The revised Form RFD-01 applies from 1 December 2026. The official FAQs on the Council's recommendations say the changes are being phased in as the system becomes ready. An excess balance in the electronic cash ledger is to be refunded automatically. These apply to new claims; claims already pending follow the existing process.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Can I now claim a refund of GST paid on input services under an inverted duty structure?
entries.a: Yes, for input tax credit on input services availed on or after 1 November 2026, under rule 89(5) as substituted by Notification 05/2026-Central Tax dated 26 October 2026. Until now, inverted duty refunds covered only credit on inputs (goods), so service businesses and manufacturers with large service costs could not recover the accumulated credit. Under the same rule, credit on capital goods availed on or after 1 April 2027 is refundable over 60 months. Credit availed before these dates is not covered.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Will GSTR-3B be locked to GSTR-1 from April 2027?
entries.a: That is the direction announced. GSTR-1, GSTR-1A and IFF are being redesigned so that the tax liability in GSTR-3B flows from what is declared in them, with new statements for reverse charge tax and input tax credit, a mechanism to correct liability and credit within the return system, and statutory backing for the Invoice Management System. CBIC has said most GST notices arise from mismatches between returns. Businesses should reconcile GSTR-1 with GSTR-3B every month now, and especially clear differences from earlier months.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Is the power to arrest under GST being removed, and what are the new penalty limits?
entries.a: The GST Council recommended removing the power to arrest, raising the threshold for prosecution from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore of tax, reducing the general penalty from Rs 50,000 to Rs 20,000 (CGST and SGST together), and allowing a reduced penalty of 5% in non-fraud cases where tax and interest are paid within 30 days of the order. These need amendments to the GST Acts and are expected from 1 April 2027. In the meantime, CBIC Instruction 02/2026-GST dated 30 October 2026 directs central GST officers to make no further arrests under GST until the amendment takes effect. State GST officers are covered only if the State issues a similar instruction. The prosecution threshold and penalty limits do not change until the amendments take effect.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Will I get a GST show-cause notice for a small amount?
entries.a: Not from central GST officers, under CBIC Instruction 02/2026-GST dated 30 October 2026. They may not issue a show-cause notice under section 73, 74 or 74A where the amount involved is below Rs 10,000, counting CGST, SGST or UTGST, IGST and compensation cess together. State GST officers are covered only if the State issues a similar instruction. The instruction is interim and does not deal with notices already issued. The GST Council also recommended an amendment to the law, expected from 1 April 2027, which is to apply to notices and appeals pending when it takes effect. Until then, any notice you receive must be answered in time.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What is the proposed annual return with quarterly payment (ARQP) scheme?
entries.a: The GST Council approved in principle an optional scheme for businesses with turnover up to Rs 5 crore in the previous year that supply only to unregistered customers, such as retailers and consumer service businesses. They would pay tax quarterly and file one annual return instead of monthly returns. The scheme has not been notified yet; the conditions, rates of interest and forms will be known only when it is.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Is the GSTR-3B late fee being waived for small businesses?
entries.a: The GST Council recommended that a business with turnover up to Rs 5 crore should pay no late fee if a delayed GSTR-3B is filed by the end of the month in which it was due. This is a recommendation and applies only once notified. Interest at 18% a year on tax paid late still applies.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Can an e-commerce seller register in another state using the platform's warehouse?
entries.a: Yes, from 1 November 2026, under new rule 14B of the CGST Rules (Notification 05/2026-Central Tax dated 26 October 2026). A person registered in a home state who supplies goods through an e-commerce operator can register in a state where they have no physical presence and declare the operator's warehouse there as the principal place of business. Output tax on supplies to registered persons, excluding those on the same PAN, must not exceed Rs 2.5 lakh a month. The operator must consent within 7 working days, Aadhaar authentication is required, and the registration is for supplies through that platform only. The application is made on the GST portal in Part B of Form GST REG-01 (GSTN Advisory No. 682 dated 1 November 2026).

entries.q: Who is treated as a non-resident (NRI) for Indian income tax?
entries.a: Under section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, an individual is resident if in India for 182 days or more in the tax year, or for 60 days in the year plus 365 days over the preceding four years. For Indian citizens and persons of Indian origin visiting India, the 60-day test becomes 182 days, or 120 days if Indian income exceeds Rs 15 lakh. An Indian citizen with Indian income above Rs 15 lakh who is not liable to tax in any other country can be deemed resident. Anyone meeting none of these tests is non-resident.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Is interest on NRE and NRO accounts taxable in India?
entries.a: Interest on an NRE account is exempt in India while the holder is a person resident outside India under FEMA (formerly section 10(4)(ii)). Interest on an NRO account is taxable, and banks generally deduct tax at 30% plus surcharge and cess under section 393(2) (formerly section 195). A lower treaty rate may apply under section 159 if the depositor provides a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 41 (formerly Form 10F).
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What tax is deducted when an NRI sells property in Mumbai?
entries.a: The buyer must deduct tax on the full sale price, not only on the capital gain, under section 393(2) (formerly section 195), and the Rs 50 lakh threshold for resident sellers does not apply. For a long-term gain the rate is 12.5% plus surcharge and cess, which is 13% to 14.95% of the price; for a short-term gain it is 30% plus surcharge and cess. On a sale price of Rs 1.2 crore with a long-term gain, TDS at 14.95% is Rs 17,94,000. From 1 October 2026, a resident individual or HUF buyer can use the PAN-based Form 141 without a TAN (Notification 121/2026); other buyers still need a TAN. The seller can apply in Form 128 (formerly Form 13) for a lower deduction certificate if the actual tax on the gain is lower.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Does an NRI need to file an income tax return in India?
entries.a: An NRI must file a return under section 263 if total Indian income exceeds the basic exemption limit, and must also file to claim a refund of excess tax deducted. Where the only income is investment income or specified long-term capital gains on which full tax was deducted, filing may not be required (section 216, formerly section 115G). Property sales usually need a return to settle the actual tax.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What is the difference between AIS and Form 26AS?
entries.a: Form 26AS mainly shows tax deducted or collected at source, advance tax and self-assessment tax against your PAN. The Annual Information Statement (section 510) is broader and also reports interest, dividends, securities and mutual fund transactions, rent and foreign remittances. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, Form 26AS is renumbered Form 168 from tax year 2026-27.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Why does my AIS not match Form 26AS or my own records?
entries.a: Common reasons include AIS showing the gross sale value of shares rather than the gain, interest reported on accrual while your passbook shows credits, duplicate entries from different reporting entities, and transactions reported under the wrong PAN. You can submit feedback on each AIS entry on the income tax portal, and the reporting entity may then correct it.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What happens if income shown in AIS is not reflected in my return?
entries.a: The department compares returns with AIS data. Unexplained differences can lead to an intimation adjusting your income, a notice, or an e-campaign communication asking for a response. Reconciling AIS, Form 26AS and your books before filing, and recording feedback on entries that are incorrect, reduces the risk of such mismatches.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What is GSTR-2B reconciliation and why does it matter now?
entries.a: GSTR-2B is the monthly auto-generated statement of input tax credit available from suppliers' filings and the Invoice Management System. Reconciling it with your purchase register identifies missing, mismatched or unfiled supplier invoices. Credit is available only where the supplier has furnished the invoice and it is communicated to you (section 16(2)(aa) of the CGST Act), and the credit table of GSTR-3B is auto-populated from GSTR-2B, so differences should be resolved before filing, not after.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: How should differences between GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and the books be handled?
entries.a: Compare outward supplies in the books with GSTR-1, and tax liability with GSTR-3B, every month. Since the July 2025 tax period, the liability auto-populated in GSTR-3B from GSTR-1, GSTR-1A and IFF cannot be edited in GSTR-3B (GSTN advisory of 7 June 2025), so errors should be corrected through GSTR-1A before GSTR-3B is filed, or in later returns. Short-paid tax should be paid with interest under section 50 of the CGST Act. Differences left unresolved commonly surface in the annual return, GSTR-9 and 9C, or in departmental scrutiny.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What is a fractional CFO?
entries.a: A fractional CFO is an experienced finance professional who works with a business for a defined number of days or hours rather than full time. The role usually covers cash flow planning, budgeting, management reporting, lender and investor information, internal controls and finance systems, for businesses needing senior finance input without a full-time appointment.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: I received an intimation after my return was processed, and the demand is wrong. What should I do?
entries.a: Compare the intimation (formerly under section 143(1)) line by line with your return; most wrong demands come from TDS not matched, a deduction or relief disallowed by the system, or a mismatch with AIS. On the income tax portal, submit a response to the outstanding demand stating that you disagree and why, and file an online rectification request with the supporting details. If rectification does not resolve it, an appeal can be filed within the time stated in the order. Do not ignore it: an unpaid demand can be adjusted against your future refunds.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: My return was marked defective. How do I respond?
entries.a: A defective return notice (formerly section 139(9)) points out an error such as a missing schedule, tax payable but not paid, or income from business shown without the required accounts. The defect must be removed by filing a corrected return in response to the notice, usually within 15 days, and an extension can be requested on the portal. If it is not corrected in time, the return is treated as if it was never filed, with the consequences of a missed return.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Can I still file my return after the due date, and what does it cost?
entries.a: A belated return can be filed up to nine months from the end of the tax year, which for FY 2025-26 is 31 December 2026. The late fee is Rs 5,000, or Rs 1,000 where total income does not exceed Rs 5 lakh, plus interest on any tax unpaid. After that, an updated return can be filed up to 48 months from the end of the following year, with additional tax of 25%, 50%, 60% or 70% of the tax and interest depending on how late it is filed. Some losses cannot be carried forward from a late return. See the compliance calendar.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: How is tax worked out when I sell a house, and how can I save it?
entries.a: A house held for more than 24 months gives a long-term gain, taxed at 12.5% without indexation; a resident individual or HUF who bought before 23 July 2024 can instead choose 20% with indexation, whichever is lower. Held for 24 months or less, the gain is added to income at slab rates. Long-term gain can be saved by buying or building another residential house in India within the time limits (exemption capped at Rs 10 crore), or by investing up to Rs 50 lakh in specified capital gains bonds within six months, locked in for five years. Amounts not reinvested before the return due date can be parked in the Capital Gains Account Scheme. NRI sellers should see the NRI taxation page for TDS and repatriation.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: How are gains on shares and mutual funds taxed?
entries.a: For listed shares and equity mutual funds on which STT is paid, gains on units held up to 12 months are taxed at 20%, and longer-held gains at 12.5% on the amount above Rs 1.25 lakh a year. Debt mutual funds bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates however long they are held. Unlisted shares held for more than 24 months are taxed at 12.5%. The gains are reported in the capital gains schedule of ITR-2 or ITR-3, and AIS shows the sale value, which must be matched with your own cost records.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Is a gift from a relative or friend taxable?
entries.a: Gifts of money or property from relatives, as defined in the income tax law (spouse, parents, children, siblings and their spouses, and certain other close relatives), are not taxed in the receiver's hands, wherever the relative lives. Gifts received on marriage, by will or inheritance are also exempt. Gifts from anyone else are fully taxable as income if their total value in the year exceeds Rs 50,000. Keep a gift deed or letter and bank records, especially for gifts from NRI relatives.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Should I choose a proprietorship, an LLP or a private limited company?
entries.a: A proprietorship is the simplest to start and is taxed at the owner's slab rates, but the owner is personally liable. An LLP limits liability, is taxed at 30% plus surcharge and cess, and needs an audit only above set turnover or contribution limits. A private limited company limits liability, can raise equity and issue shares to employees, can opt for a lower tax rate of 22% plus surcharge and cess, but must have its accounts audited every year and file more returns with the ROC. The right choice depends on liability, funding plans, the number of owners and the cost of compliance.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What is the GST composition scheme, and who can opt for it?
entries.a: The composition scheme lets small businesses pay GST at a fixed low rate on turnover and file simpler returns: 1% for traders and manufacturers, 5% for restaurants, and 6% for eligible service providers. It is available to businesses with turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore in the previous year (Rs 50 lakh for service providers). A composition dealer cannot charge GST on invoices, cannot claim input tax credit, and cannot make inter-state supplies of goods. It suits businesses selling mainly to consumers.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Is GST payable on rent?
entries.a: Renting a residential unit for use as a residence is exempt, except where it is let to a GST-registered person, who then pays 18% GST under reverse charge. Renting commercial property is taxable at 18% if the landlord is registered; where the landlord is unregistered and the tenant is registered, the tenant pays the tax under reverse charge. A landlord whose rent and other taxable supplies exceed Rs 20 lakh a year must register. For housing society maintenance charges, see housing society services.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Who has to issue e-invoices under GST?
entries.a: E-invoicing applies to a business whose aggregate turnover has exceeded Rs 5 crore in any financial year since 2017-18, for invoices and credit and debit notes issued to registered buyers and for exports. Once applicable, it continues even if turnover later falls. Businesses with turnover of Rs 10 crore or more must report invoices on the invoice registration portal within 30 days of the invoice date. A buyer cannot claim input tax credit on an invoice that should have been an e-invoice but was not.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: What is Udyam registration, and what is the 45-day payment rule?
entries.a: Udyam registration is the free, online MSME registration on the government portal, using Aadhaar and PAN. Since April 2025, a micro enterprise has investment up to Rs 2.5 crore and turnover up to Rs 10 crore, and a small enterprise up to Rs 25 crore and Rs 100 crore. Buyers must pay registered micro and small suppliers within the agreed credit period, not exceeding 45 days, or 15 days where none is agreed; otherwise the buyer cannot deduct the expense for tax until the year it is paid (formerly section 43B(h)), and owes interest to the supplier.
entries.t: Knowledge and frequently asked questions

entries.q: Can AI be trusted with accounting work?

entries.q: What is the difference between a forensic audit and a statutory audit?
entries.a: A statutory audit gives an opinion on whether financial statements are fairly presented, using sampling and materiality. entries.q: What is the difference between GSTR-2A and GSTR-2B?
entries.a: GSTR-2A is a dynamic statement that changes whenever a supplier files or amends GSTR-1. GSTR-2B is a static monthly statement generated for each return period, and it is the basis on which input tax credit in GSTR-3B is checked.

entries.q: What is the Invoice Management System (IMS)?

entries.q: What is DRC-01C?

entries.q: How much TDS does a buyer deduct when an NRI sells property?

entries.q: What is RNOR status?

entries.q: What happens to an NRE account after returning to India?

entries.q: How do I convert an NRE or NRO account to a resident account?
entries.a: Tell each bank in writing soon after you arrive, using its change of residential status form, and give your date of return. entries.q: What happens to an NRO account after returning to India?
entries.a: It is redesignated as an ordinary resident savings or current account. The balance stays in rupees and, unlike an NRE balance, cannot be moved to an RFC account. Interest remains taxable as before, but once the bank records you as a resident, tax is deducted at resident rates instead of the higher non-resident rates. Ask the bank for an interest certificate split between the two periods.

entries.q: Is interest on an NRE fixed deposit taxable after returning to India?
entries.a: Yes, for interest that accrues after you become a person resident in India under FEMA. The exemption for NRE interest (formerly section 10(4)(ii)) applies only while you are a person resident outside India under FEMA. This is so even if you are still RNOR for income tax. Interest up to the date of return stays exempt, so keep the bank's statement showing the date of redesignation.

entries.q: Is there a penalty for not converting an NRE account after returning to India?
entries.a: Continuing an NRE account after you become a FEMA resident is a contravention of the FEMA deposit regulations. A penalty can be up to three times the amount involved where it can be quantified, or up to Rs 2 lakh where it cannot. A late conversion is usually regularised by redesignating the account and, where needed, applying for compounding. Interest claimed as exempt after the date of return may also have to be offered to tax.

entries.q: What happens to an FCNR deposit after returning to India?

entries.q: Which structure should a foreign company use in India?
entries.a: It depends on what the business will do in India. A private limited subsidiary suits most operating businesses because it can carry on the full range of permitted activities and is taxed as an Indian company. A liaison office only represents the parent and cannot earn income. A branch office can carry on specified activities and is taxed as part of the foreign company. A project office is tied to a particular contract in India. The options are compared on sector rules, tax, repatriation and exit before a decision is taken.
entries.t: Foreign companies and businesses in India

entries.q: Can a foreign company own 100% of an Indian company?
entries.a: In many sectors, yes, under the automatic route of the foreign direct investment rules. Some sectors have caps or conditions, some are prohibited, and some need government approval. Investors from countries sharing a land border with India have separate approval requirements. A private limited company needs at least two shareholders, so a nominee commonly holds one share for the parent.
entries.t: Foreign companies and businesses in India

entries.q: Does an Indian subsidiary need a director living in India?
entries.a: Yes. A private limited company needs at least two directors, and at least one director must have stayed in India for 182 days or more during the financial year, under section 149(3) of the Companies Act, 2013.
entries.t: Foreign companies and businesses in India

entries.q: What has to be reported after foreign money comes into the Indian company?
entries.a: The money must come through banking channels, and shares must be issued within the time allowed. The allotment is reported in Form FC-GPR through the authorised dealer bank within 30 days of allotment. A Foreign Liabilities and Assets (FLA) return is then filed with the RBI by 15 July each year.
entries.t: Foreign companies and businesses in India

entries.q: How is tax handled on payments to the foreign parent?
entries.a: The Indian payer generally deducts tax under section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (formerly section 195), at the rate in the Act or the tax treaty, where the treaty is available and beneficial. A treaty claim needs a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 41 (formerly Form 10F). Remittances are supported by Form 145 and, where required, the accountant's certificate in Form 146 (formerly Forms 15CA and 15CB). Payments between related parties also have to meet transfer pricing rules.

entries.q: Can this be handled without being in India?
entries.a: Largely, yes. Calls, document review, filings and accounting are handled remotely. Founders' identity and company documents usually have to be notarised or apostilled in the home country and sent to India, and the required signatures are obtained digitally where the law allows.

Member contributions are generally not taxable under the principle of mutuality, but interest, rent from mobile towers and hoardings, and other income from outsiders can be taxable, subject to deductions available to co-operative societies.
entries.t: Co-operative housing society accounting and audit

entries.q: Can the same firm do the accounting and the audit?
entries.a: No. An auditor cannot audit accounts that the same firm has prepared. A society can engage the firm for monthly accounting and appoint a different auditor, or appoint the firm as auditor and keep its own accountant.
entries.t: Co-operative housing society accounting and audit

entries.q: Co-operative housing society accounting and audit

entries.q: Can an Indian chartered accountant keep books for a business outside India?
entries.a: Yes. Bookkeeping, month-end close, management reporting and financial modelling can be done remotely in your own accounting system, such as QuickBooks Online, Xero or Zoho Books, following your country's accounting conventions. Statutory audit and tax filings that your local law reserves for locally licensed professionals remain with your local accountant, and the work is coordinated with them.
entries.t: Remote accounting, CFO and finance automation for businesses outside India

entries.q: Which time zones do you cover?
entries.a: India Standard Time overlaps with most of the working day in Singapore, Malaysia and Hong Kong, the full working day in the UAE and East Africa, the afternoon in Australia, the morning in the UK and Europe, and the early morning or late evening in the US. Weekly calls are scheduled in your time zone.
entries.t: Remote accounting, CFO and finance automation for businesses outside India

entries.q: How is work shared securely?
entries.a: Work is done in your cloud accounting system with a user login you control, and documents are exchanged through a shared drive with access limited to the people involved. A confidentiality clause is part of every engagement letter.
entries.t: Remote accounting, CFO and finance automation for businesses outside India

entries.q: How are fees agreed and paid?
entries.a: Scope and fees are agreed in writing in an engagement letter before work begins, usually as a fixed monthly fee for recurring work. Invoices can be raised in US dollars, pounds, euros or dirhams and paid by international bank transfer.
entries.t: Remote accounting, CFO and finance automation for businesses outside India

entries.q: Do you help foreign companies doing business in India?
entries.a: Yes. Support covers Indian tax on payments to and from India, TDS on payments to non-residents and treaty relief, GST on cross-border services, and coordination of company and regulatory filings for an Indian subsidiary or branch with the relevant specialists.
entries.t: Remote accounting, CFO and finance automation for businesses outside India

entries.q: Do you work with businesses in Singapore?
entries.a: Yes. Bookkeeping, month-end close, management reporting, financial models and finance automation are provided remotely to businesses in Singapore and South-East Asia, along with the Indian tax side of payments between India and Singapore under the India-Singapore tax treaty. Singapore statutory filings and audits stay with local corporate secretaries, tax agents and auditors.

entries.q: Which regime is the default for tax year 2026-27?
entries.a: The new regime is the default. An individual without business income can choose the old regime in the return each year. One with business or professional income can switch back to the old regime only once.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: Up to what income is no tax payable under the new regime?
entries.a: A resident individual with total income up to Rs 12 lakh pays no tax under the new regime because of the rebate. For a salaried person, the standard deduction of Rs 75,000 takes this to Rs 12.75 lakh of salary. Income taxed at special rates, such as capital gains, does not get the rebate.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: Who has to pay advance tax?
entries.a: Anyone whose tax for the year, after TDS and TCS, is Rs 10,000 or more. A resident senior citizen with no business or professional income is exempt.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: What are the advance tax due dates?
entries.a: 15% of the tax by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March. Taxpayers under presumptive taxation for business or profession can pay the full amount by 15 March.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: How much TDS does a buyer deduct when buying property from an NRI?
entries.a: For property held for more than 24 months, 12.5% plus surcharge and 4% cess, on the full sale price unless the seller has a lower deduction certificate. For property held for 24 months or less, the rate is 30% plus surcharge and cess.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: Does the buyer need a TAN?
entries.a: From 1 October 2026, a buyer who is a resident individual or HUF can deduct and deposit TDS on property bought from a non-resident using a PAN-based challan-cum-statement, without a TAN. Companies and firms still need a TAN.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: What is the interest on late TDS?
entries.a: 1% a month from the date tax should have been deducted to the date it was deducted, and 1.5% a month from the date of deduction to the date of deposit. A part of a month counts as a full month.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: What is the interest on late GST payment?
entries.a: 18% a year on the tax paid late through the cash ledger, counted in days from the day after the due date to the date of payment.
entries.t: Tax calculators for tax year 2026-27

entries.q: What should I do first when I receive a GST notice?
entries.a: Note the form number, section, tax period, amount and reply date, and check that the notice appears on the GST portal under View Notices and Orders. Then compare the figures with your books and returns. Do not ignore it or pay only because a notice has arrived: first work out whether the difference is real. A missed date can lead to an order without your side being heard.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: How do I reply to an ASMT-10 notice?
entries.a: ASMT-10 lists differences found on scrutiny of your returns under section 61. Reply in Form ASMT-11 within 30 days of service, or any further period the officer allows. Accept and pay what is genuinely short-paid, using DRC-03, and explain the rest with a reconciliation and documents. If the explanation is accepted, the officer closes the matter in ASMT-12. If not, proceedings under section 73, 74 or 74A can follow.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: What is DRC-01A, and do I have to reply?
entries.a: DRC-01A is an intimation that an officer may send before a show cause notice, under rule 142(1A), stating the tax, interest and penalty the officer has worked out. It is an opportunity to settle or correct the matter early. Reply in Part B by the date given, with payment through DRC-03 or your submissions. The officer may not issue it in every case, because it has been optional for officers since 2020.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: How do I reply to a DRC-01 show cause notice?
entries.a: DRC-01 is the summary of a show cause notice. Reply in DRC-06 on the portal by the date in the notice, dealing with each ground, attaching reconciliations and documents, and asking for a personal hearing. Under section 75(4), a hearing must be given where you ask for one or where an adverse decision is contemplated, and Circular 258/04/2026-GST says officers may grant up to four hearings. Read the attached notice as well as the summary, since the grounds are usually set out there.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: What is the difference between DRC-01B and DRC-01C?
entries.a: DRC-01B (rule 88C) is issued when tax reported in GSTR-1 exceeds tax paid in GSTR-3B beyond a set limit. DRC-01C (rule 88D) is issued when ITC claimed in GSTR-3B exceeds ITC available in GSTR-2B beyond a set limit. In both, you have 7 days to pay or explain in Part B. If you do neither, filing of GSTR-1 or IFF for later periods is blocked until you respond.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: What is the time limit for a GST notice?
entries.a: For FY 2023-24 and earlier, section 73 orders are due within 3 years of the annual return due date, with the notice at least 3 months earlier, and section 74 orders within 5 years, with the notice at least 6 months earlier. From FY 2024-25, section 74A allows a notice within 42 months of the annual return due date and an order within 12 months of the notice. FY 2022-23 section 73 orders are due by 31 December 2026.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: Can the penalty on a GST notice be reduced by paying early?
entries.a: Yes. Under section 73, paying tax and interest before the notice or within 30 days of it means no penalty, otherwise the penalty is the higher of 10% of tax or Rs 10,000. Under section 74, the penalty is 15% if paid before the notice, 25% within 30 days of it, 50% within 30 days of the order, and otherwise 100%. Under section 74A, the periods are 60 days: no penalty in non-fraud cases, and 15%, 25% or 50% in fraud cases.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: Why did I get a notice for a GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch?
entries.a: Credit is available only where the supplier has reported the invoice and it appears in your GSTR-2B, under section 16(2)(aa). Claiming more in GSTR-3B than GSTR-2B shows can bring DRC-01C, ASMT-10 or a show cause notice. The reply needs an invoice-wise reconciliation showing timing differences, credits taken in another period and supplier failures, with payment or reversal of credit that cannot be supported. GST reconciliation.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: What happens if I do not reply to a GST notice?
entries.a: The officer can pass an order on the available record, summarised in DRC-07. Under section 78, the amount is generally due within 3 months of service of the order, after which recovery under section 79 can begin, including from your bank account, debtors or property. The officer can require earlier payment in the interest of revenue, for reasons recorded in writing.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: How do I appeal against a GST order in DRC-07?
entries.a: File Form APL-01 within 3 months of the order being communicated. The appellate authority can allow one more month for sufficient cause. You must pay the admitted amount in full and 10% of the disputed tax, capped at Rs 20 crore. For an order demanding only a penalty, the pre-deposit is 10% of the penalty. Once the appeal is filed with the pre-deposit, recovery of the balance is stayed under section 107(7).
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: Can I get a GST notice after my registration is cancelled?
entries.a: Yes. Under section 29(3), cancellation of registration does not affect liability for tax and other dues for the period before cancellation, so notices can still be issued within the time limit. Keep your portal login, email and mobile number active and keep your records, because notices continue to be issued on the portal.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: Is a GST notice issued for tax below Rs 10,000?
entries.a: Not by central GST officers, under CBIC Instruction 02/2026-GST dated 30 October 2026. They may not issue a show cause notice under section 73, 74 or 74A where the amount is below Rs 10,000, counting CGST, SGST or UTGST, IGST and cess together. State officers are covered only if the State issues a similar instruction. The instruction is interim, so answer any notice you do receive in time, and cite the instruction in your reply where it applies.
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: What must a section 74 fraud notice show?
entries.a: CBIC Circular 258/04/2026-GST dated 26 October 2026 says allegations of fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression must rest on specific evidence and intent to evade tax, set out in the notice. Non-payment or a discrepancy alone is not enough. If fraud is not established, the demand is to be confined to the non-fraud provisions. The circular also calls for reasoned orders, and an order cannot exceed the notice or rest on new grounds under section 75(7).
entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.t: GST notices: what each form means and how to reply

entries.q: Is GSTR-9 mandatory for turnover under Rs 2 crore?
entries.a: No. Notification 15/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025 exempts registered persons with aggregate turnover up to Rs 2 crore. Above that, GSTR-9 is required, except for classes outside section 44 such as input service distributors, tax deductors and collectors, casual taxable persons and non-resident taxable persons.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: Who has to file GSTR-9C?
entries.a: GSTR-9C is required where aggregate turnover for the year exceeds Rs 5 crore. It is a self-certified statement reconciling the annual return with the audited financial statements, and certification by a chartered accountant has not been required since the 2021 change to section 44.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: What is the last date to claim ITC for FY 2025-26?
entries.a: Under section 16(4), ITC for FY 2025-26 can be claimed only up to 30 November 2026 or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier. If you file GSTR-9 before 30 November, the window closes on that date. Complete the GSTR-2B reconciliation and claim what is due in the October 2026 GSTR-3B before then.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: Can I claim missed ITC through GSTR-9?
entries.a: No. GSTR-9 is a statement of what was reported during the year and cannot be used to take new credit. Missed ITC must be claimed in GSTR-3B within the section 16(4) time limit. If the annual return shows that tax was underpaid, pay it through DRC-03.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: Can GSTR-9 be revised after filing?
entries.a: No. There is no facility to revise GSTR-9 after it is filed, so reconcile before filing. Differences found later are generally dealt with through DRC-03 for extra tax, and they may be raised on scrutiny or by notice.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: What is the late fee for GSTR-9?
entries.a: Under Notification 07/2023-Central Tax, the total CGST and SGST fee is Rs 50 per day for turnover up to Rs 5 crore, Rs 100 per day from Rs 5 crore to Rs 20 crore, and Rs 200 per day above Rs 20 crore, subject to caps linked to turnover in the State or Union territory. There is also a risk of notice under section 46 and best judgement assessment if the return is not filed.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: Why does GSTR-9 lead to GST notices?
entries.a: Officers compare GSTR-9 with GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, GSTR-2B and e-way bill data. Differences left unexplained often lead to ASMT-10 or a show cause notice, and the annual return due date also starts the time limit for those notices. See GST notices and how to reply.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: What is the revised GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C procedure for FY 2025-26?
entries.a: Filing is on the GST portal in the usual way, once all GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns for the year are filed. Notification 05/2026-Central Tax dated 26 October 2026 extends the simplified reporting options, such as combining certain tables, to FY 2025-26 onwards. Read the current instructions on the portal for each table before filing.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: What records do I need for GSTR-9?
entries.a: Keep GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and GSTR-2B for April 2025 to March 2026, and the amendments reported up to the cut-off in the following year. You also need sales and purchase registers, debit and credit notes, ITC reversal workings, HSN-wise summaries, DRC-03 challans, and audited or draft financial statements.
entries.t: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks

entries.q: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: dates, limits and checks
entries.a: GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26: due date 31 December 2026, Rs 2 crore and Rs 5 crore limits, 30 November ITC cut-off, late fee and pre-filing checks. Borivali West, Mumbai.

entries.q: What are the new GST registration rules effective from 1 November 2026?
entries.a: Notification 05/2026-Central Tax dated 26 October 2026 revises Form REG-01 and rule 19 on amendments, adds rule 14B for e-commerce sellers, and substitutes rules 20 and 21 on cancellation. Circular 257/03/2026-GST gives officers document lists and limits on queries. Registration is generally processed in 7 working days with Aadhaar authentication and 30 days otherwise, and is deemed approved under rule 9 if the time is missed. Revised suspension and cancellation procedures follow from 1 April 2027.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the changes in GST REG-01 from November 2026?
entries.a: Form REG-01 is substituted from 1 November 2026. It now has options for registration under rules 14A and 14B, fields for the e-commerce operator's warehouse, a nature of business for supplies made only through an operator, and drop-down document lists. A new Form REG-05A intimates a deemed rejection where the applicant does not respond to a notice or verification.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What is the new Rule 14B simplified GST registration scheme?
entries.a: Under rule 14B, inserted by Notification 05/2026-Central Tax from 1 November 2026, a person registered in one State who supplies goods through an e-commerce operator can register in a State with no physical presence, declaring the operator's warehouse as the principal place of business. Output tax on supplies to registered persons, excluding those on the same PAN, must not exceed Rs 2.5 lakh a month. The operator must consent within 7 working days, Aadhaar authentication is required, and the registration covers supplies through that platform only.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: Can e-commerce sellers obtain GST registration without a physical presence in the destination state?
entries.a: Yes, under rule 14B from 1 November 2026, if goods are supplied through an e-commerce operator whose warehouse in that State is declared as the principal place of business, the seller is registered in a home State and the Rs 2.5 lakh monthly limit on output tax on supplies to registered persons is met. The application is made in Form REG-01 with the operator's consent. See the full answer.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What is the new automatic GST registration cancellation process under REG-16?
entries.a: From 1 November 2026, under rule 20 and a GSTN advisory, a compliant REG-16 application can be approved by the system. All returns due must be filed. Composition taxpayers, non-resident and OIDAR taxpayers and ISDs are cancelled electronically once returns are filed. Regular, casual and SEZ taxpayers are too, where output tax is up to Rs 2.5 lakh in every period. Above that, GSTR-10 must be filed within 3 days of the stated date, or the application goes to the officer. A revised REG-16 applies from 1 December 2026.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the changes in GST registration amendment under REG-14?
entries.a: From 1 November 2026, Form REG-14 and rule 19 are substituted. Amendments are to be applied for within 15 days of the change, and most take effect automatically on filing. A change of principal place of business goes to the officer, with automatic amendment for rule 14A registrants from 1 December 2026. Composition taxpayers can also update their category through REG-14, across all GSTINs on the same PAN.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the new GST TDS provisions applicable to scrap dealers?
entries.a: From 1 November 2026, Notification 07/2026-Central Tax requires a registered buyer to deduct GST TDS under section 51 on purchases of the listed goods from registered suppliers, where the contract value exceeds Rs 2.5 lakh. The buyer needs separate TDS registration in Form REG-07 and files GSTR-7 by the 10th of the following month. Notification 06/2026-Central Tax also withdraws the registration exemption for suppliers of these goods.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: Is GST TDS applicable to used cooking oil, plastic scrap, tyre scrap and e-waste?
entries.a: Yes, from 1 November 2026, when bought by a registered person from a registered supplier. The goods are used cooking oil (heading 1518), waste and scrap of plastics (3915), waste and scrap of tyres (4004), metal scrap (Chapters 72 to 81, already covered) and electrical and electronic waste (8549). If the supplier is unregistered, TDS does not apply, and the buyer pays tax under reverse charge instead (Notification 04/2026-Central Tax (Rate)).
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What is the 2% GST TDS requirement on scrap purchases above Rs 2.5 lakh?
entries.a: The buyer deducts 2% of the taxable value, excluding GST: 1% CGST and 1% SGST on supplies within a State, or 2% IGST on inter-State supplies. It applies only where the total value of supply under one contract exceeds Rs 2.5 lakh. The amount is deposited and reported in GSTR-7 by the 10th of the following month.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the new GST composition scheme categories from November 2026?
entries.a: Under Notification 05/2026-Central Tax, Table 5 of Forms CMP-02 and CMP-04 now lists manufacturers (other than of notified goods), restaurant and catering suppliers under paragraph 6(b) of Schedule II, other persons eligible under section 10(1), and persons eligible under section 10(2A). The section 10(2A) category cannot be selected together with the section 10(1) categories. Forms CMP-08 and GSTR-4 also change from 1 November 2026, to report goods, services and section 9(5) supplies separately.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the new GST rules for post-sale discounts from 1 November?
entries.a: From 1 November 2026, under Notification 03/2026-Central Tax, section 15(3)(b) is substituted. A discount given after supply is excluded from taxable value if the supplier issues a credit note under section 34 and the recipient reverses the related ITC. Section 34 now lists post-sale discount as a ground for a credit note. The earlier conditions on an agreement made at or before the supply no longer apply.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: Can a supplier issue a GST credit note without a prior agreement for post-sale discounts?
entries.a: Yes, from 1 November 2026. A prior agreement is no longer required for the discount to reduce taxable value. The supplier cannot reduce output tax, however, if a registered recipient has not reversed the ITC on the credit note, or where the tax burden has been passed on to another person. The time limit in section 34(2) continues to apply. Check supplies made before 1 November 2026 separately.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the new GST refund rules for inverted duty structure?
entries.a: Under rule 89(5), as substituted by Notification 05/2026-Central Tax, ITC on input services availed on or after 1 November 2026 is included in inverted duty refunds. ITC on capital goods availed on or after 1 April 2027 is refundable over 60 months. Earlier credit is not covered. See the full answer.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: Can 90% of an inverted duty structure refund be sanctioned provisionally?
entries.a: Yes. From 1 November 2026, under section 54(6) as amended and the rules, 90% of an inverted duty or zero-rated refund can be sanctioned provisionally through the portal on a risk-based check, within 3 working days of acknowledgement. The changes are being phased in as the system becomes ready, and the revised Form RFD-01 applies from 1 December 2026.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What is the new 10-day GST refund acknowledgement requirement?
entries.a: Under rules 90 and 91 as amended from 1 November 2026, the department must issue an acknowledgement or a deficiency memo within 10 days instead of 15, failing which the application is treated as acknowledged. This applies to new claims. Claims already pending follow the existing process.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What is the revised GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C filing procedure for FY 2025-26?
entries.a: The simplified reporting options are extended to FY 2025-26 onwards by Notification 05/2026-Central Tax. All GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns must be filed first, and the due date is 31 December 2026. See GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C for FY 2025-26.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the GST return filing due dates for November 2026?
entries.a: For the October 2026 period, GSTR-7 and GSTR-8 are due on 10 November, GSTR-1 on 11 November, IFF and GSTR-6 on 13 November, GSTR-3B for monthly filers on 20 November, and PMT-06 for QRMP taxpayers on 25 November 2026. The November 2026 period falls due on the same days of December.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What is the proposed 14-digit E-Way Bill number?
entries.a: A GSTN advisory dated 4 November 2026 says e-way bill numbers will go from 12 to 14 digits, and consolidated e-way bill numbers from 10 to 11 digits, as the present numbers are running out. Businesses using ERP systems or APIs should update fields and validation rules to accept the longer numbers.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: When will the new E-Way Bill numbering system be implemented?
entries.a: From 1 January 2027, according to the GSTN advisory of 4 November 2026. The changes are to appear in the sandbox first, so that software can be tested, and further technical details are to be published on the e-way bill portal.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: What are the GST changes applicable from 1 November 2026 and 1 January 2027?
entries.a: From 1 November 2026: new registration forms and rules, rule 14B, post-sale discounts, refund changes, TDS on specified scrap and revised composition forms. From 1 January 2027: the new e-way bill numbering, e-invoice schema with codes for reverse charge self-invoices (Notifications 04/2026 and 05/2026-Central Tax), and revised GSTR-7A. Between them, revised REG-16 and RFD-01 apply from 1 December 2026.
entries.t: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027

entries.q: GST updates: changes from October 2026 to January 2027
entries.a: GST changes from 1 November 2026 and 1 January 2027: REG-01, rule 14B, REG-16, TDS on scrap, post-sale discounts, refunds, Circulars 257 to 266, e-way bill numbers.
