entries.q: Who qualifies as an NRI under Indian Income Tax rules?
entries.a: Tax law uses the term non-resident. Under section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, an individual is non-resident for a tax year if none of the residence tests is met. The basic tests are 182 days or more in India in the year, or 60 days in the year plus 365 days over the preceding four years. Indian citizens and persons of Indian origin have relaxed tests. FEMA has its own separate test, which governs bank accounts.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How many days can an NRI stay in India without becoming a resident?
entries.a: For an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin on a visit, the usual limit is under 182 days in the tax year. If Indian income, excluding foreign sources, exceeds Rs 15 lakh, you become resident at 120 days if you also spent 365 days in India over the preceding four years. An Indian citizen with Indian income above Rs 15 lakh who is not liable to tax in any other country can be deemed resident regardless of days.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What happens if an NRI stays in India for more than 182 days?
entries.a: At 182 days or more in a tax year, you are resident for that year. You may still be Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR), in which case most foreign income stays outside Indian tax. Once you are resident and ordinarily resident, your worldwide income is taxable and foreign assets must be reported in the return. Your bank account status follows FEMA, not this test.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How is NRI residential status calculated?
entries.a: Count the days of physical presence in India in the tax year, 1 April to 31 March, and the days in the preceding four years, using passport stamps. Apply the 182-day and 60-day tests with the relaxations for citizens and persons of Indian origin. If you are resident, then check RNOR: non-resident in 9 of the preceding 10 years, or 729 days or less in India in the preceding 7 years. Status is decided afresh each year.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is the difference between NRI, RNOR and Resident?
entries.a: A non-resident is taxed in India only on income earned, received or arising in India. An RNOR is also generally taxed on Indian income only, plus foreign income from a business controlled or profession set up in India. A resident and ordinarily resident is taxed on worldwide income, can claim foreign tax credit, and must report foreign assets in Schedule FA.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Does an NRI have to pay income tax in India?
entries.a: Yes, on income earned or received in India, such as rent, capital gains on Indian assets, NRO interest, dividends and Indian salary. NRE interest is exempt while you are a person resident outside India under FEMA. The rebate that makes income up to a set level tax-free for residents is not available to non-residents, so tax can arise on smaller amounts.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is foreign salary taxable in India for an NRI?
entries.a: Salary for work done outside India and received outside India is not taxable in India for a non-resident. Salary for work done in India is taxable, wherever it is paid. Salary first received in India, including into an NRE account directly from an employer, can also become taxable, so have it paid abroad and then remit it.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is income earned outside India taxable in India?
entries.a: Not for a non-resident, unless it is received or deemed to be received in India. The same generally holds for an RNOR, except income from a business controlled or a profession set up in India. Money you remit to India from income already earned abroad is not income when it arrives.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What happens to my tax status when I return permanently to India?
entries.a: Income tax status changes by the day count, and is often RNOR for the first years, so foreign income can stay outside Indian tax for that period. It then becomes resident and ordinarily resident. FEMA status changes earlier, from the day you return for work, business or an uncertain stay, and your NRE and NRO accounts must be redesignated. See returning to India.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How does the new Income Tax Act, 2025 affect NRIs?
entries.a: The Act applies from 1 April 2026 and uses tax year in place of previous year and assessment year. The residence tests in section 6 are carried over. Many section and form numbers change: for example, TDS on non-residents is section 393(2) (formerly section 195), treaty relief is section 159 (formerly section 90), and Form 10F is now Form 41. Income up to 31 March 2026 stays under the old Act.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is it mandatory for an NRI to file an income tax return in India?
entries.a: It is required if total Indian income exceeds the basic exemption limit, which for FY 2025-26 is Rs 4 lakh under the new regime. You must also file to claim a TDS refund, and usually after selling property. Where the only income is investment income or specified long-term gains with full tax deducted, filing may not be required (section 216, formerly section 115G).
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI file an income tax return from abroad?
entries.a: Register on the income tax e-filing portal with your PAN, overseas mobile and email. Download AIS and Form 26AS, work out Indian income and TDS, select non-resident status and give the days spent in India. File online and verify the return. A pre-validated Indian bank account is needed for a refund.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Which ITR form should an NRI use?
entries.a: Most NRIs use ITR-2, which covers salary, house property, capital gains and other sources. ITR-3 applies if there is business or professional income in India. ITR-1 and ITR-4 are for residents only. Filing the wrong form can lead to a defective return notice and delay any refund.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI file an income tax return without visiting India?
entries.a: Yes. Filing and verification are done online, and most notices are answered online too. You do not need to travel or give a power of attorney to file a return, though your Indian mobile or bank details make verification easier.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can a Chartered Accountant file my Indian tax return while I am overseas?
entries.a: Yes. A chartered accountant can prepare the computation from your documents and file it through the portal, with your authorisation. You still verify the return yourself, and you remain responsible for its contents.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What documents are required for NRI income tax return filing?
entries.a: PAN and portal login, passport pages showing travel dates, AIS and Form 26AS, and TDS certificates. Add NRO and NRE statements with interest certificates, rent agreements, capital gains statements, purchase and sale deeds for property, and a Tax Residency Certificate with Form 41 if claiming treaty relief. Also keep details of an Indian bank account for the refund.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is the due date for NRI income tax return filing?
entries.a: For FY 2025-26, the due date was 31 July 2026 for most individuals without business income and 31 August 2026 for business cases not subject to audit. Audit cases have until 21 November 2026. A belated return can be filed up to 31 December 2026 with a late fee. See the compliance calendar for current dates.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI claim a refund of excess TDS?
entries.a: Yes, by filing the return for that year and showing the actual tax on your income. This is common on property sales, NRO interest and mutual fund gains, because TDS is often higher than the final tax. The refund goes to a pre-validated bank account in your name, so validate the account before filing.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI verify an income tax return from abroad?
entries.a: Use an electronic verification code through a pre-validated Indian bank or demat account, net banking, or Aadhaar OTP if your Aadhaar is linked to a working mobile. Otherwise, sign the ITR-V and send it by post to CPC, Bengaluru, to reach within 30 days of filing. A return that is not verified is treated as not filed.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What happens if an NRI does not file an income tax return?
entries.a: You lose any refund of excess TDS, and some losses cannot be carried forward. If tax is due, interest and a late fee of up to Rs 5,000 apply, and the department may issue a notice. For a missed year, an updated return can be filed within the time allowed, with additional tax. See late returns.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is the tax on the sale of property by an NRI in India?
entries.a: Property held for more than 24 months gives a long-term gain, taxed at 12.5% without indexation, plus surcharge and cess. Property held for 24 months or less gives a short-term gain, taxed at slab rates. The option of the older indexed method for property bought before 23 July 2024 is limited to residents. Exemptions for reinvestment may reduce the tax.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How much TDS should be deducted when buying property from an NRI?
entries.a: On the full sale price, under section 393(2): 12.5% plus surcharge and cess for a long-term gain, which comes to 13% to 14.95%, and 30% plus surcharge and cess for a short-term gain. The Rs 50 lakh limit for resident sellers does not apply. From 1 October 2026, resident individual and HUF buyers can use PAN-based Form 141 without a TAN. Try the calculator.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI avoid excessive TDS on the sale of property?
entries.a: Yes, by obtaining a lower or nil deduction certificate before the sale, because TDS is otherwise on the price and not on the gain. The buyer then deducts at the rate in the certificate. Without a certificate, the excess can only be recovered through a refund after filing the return.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI obtain a lower TDS certificate?
entries.a: Apply online in Form 128 (formerly Form 13) under section 395 on TRACES, with a capital gains computation, purchase and sale documents, the buyer's details and earlier returns. Your PAN and TRACES registration must be in order. The officer can raise queries, and it can take several weeks, so apply well before the sale date.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How is capital gains tax calculated on the sale of property by an NRI?
entries.a: Start with the sale price, or the stamp duty value if higher beyond the permitted margin. Deduct transfer costs such as brokerage, then the purchase cost and improvement cost. For property bought before 1 April 2001, fair market value on that date can replace cost. There is no indexation for non-residents on current sales. Then apply 12.5% or slab rates, plus surcharge and cess.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI claim exemption under Section 54?
entries.a: Yes. An NRI can claim the exemption now in section 82 (formerly section 54) on a long-term gain from a residential house by buying a house in India within one year before or two years after the sale, or building one within three years. It is capped at Rs 10 crore. Section 85 (formerly section 54EC) allows up to Rs 50 lakh in specified bonds within six months. Unused amounts go to a capital gains account by the return due date.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What happens if the buyer deducts excess TDS?
entries.a: The seller claims the excess as a refund by filing the return for that year. Check that the buyer has filed the TDS statement and that the credit appears in Form 26AS. If the buyer has deducted but not reported it correctly, the buyer must correct the statement, because credit generally follows Form 26AS.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI get a refund of TDS deducted on property sale?
entries.a: File an income tax return for the year of sale showing the actual capital gain and any exemption claimed. Keep the purchase and sale deeds and proof of costs. Pre-validate an Indian bank account for the refund and verify the return. The refund comes after processing, and any queries are raised online.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI sell inherited property in India?
entries.a: Yes. For capital gains, the previous owner's cost and holding period are counted, so most inherited property gives a long-term gain. Keep the will or succession document and the original purchase papers. TDS applies in the usual way. Proceeds can be remitted from the NRO account within the USD 1 million yearly limit.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI repatriate property sale proceeds abroad?
entries.a: Credit the proceeds to your NRO account and remit up to USD 1 million per financial year, after paying tax. Your bank will generally need Forms 145 and 146 (formerly 15CA and 15CB). Where the property was bought from NRE or foreign funds, separate repatriation rules apply, limited to the foreign exchange paid and to two residential properties. Check the details with your bank first.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is interest earned on an NRE account taxable in India?
entries.a: No, while you are a person resident outside India under FEMA. The exemption stops once you become a FEMA resident, even if you are still RNOR for income tax. It may be taxable in your country of residence, so check the rules there.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is interest on an NRO account taxable?
entries.a: Yes. It is taxable in India, and banks generally deduct TDS at 30% plus surcharge and cess. A lower rate may apply under a tax treaty if you give the bank a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 41. You can claim any excess back by filing a return.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is the difference between NRE and NRO accounts?
entries.a: An NRE account holds foreign earnings in rupees, is fully repatriable, and its interest is exempt in India. An NRO account holds income earned in India, such as rent and dividends. Its interest is taxable, and repatriation is limited to USD 1 million a financial year. NRE accounts can be joint only with another NRI, or with a resident on a former-or-survivor basis.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI claim a refund of TDS deducted on NRO interest?
entries.a: Yes, if your actual tax is lower than the TDS, by filing a return for the year. This often helps where total Indian income is small or a treaty rate applies. Check that the bank's TDS appears in Form 26AS before filing.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI transfer money from an NRO account to an overseas account?
entries.a: Yes, up to USD 1 million per financial year, for current income and sale proceeds, once tax has been paid. Your bank will generally ask for Forms 145 and 146 (formerly 15CA and 15CB). Rent, dividends and similar current income can usually be remitted within this process.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What are the tax implications of converting an NRO account into an NRE account?
entries.a: An NRO account is not converted into an NRE account as such. You can transfer funds from NRO to NRE only within the USD 1 million yearly limit, after tax is paid, with the same forms as a remittance. The transfer itself is not income. Interest on that money becomes exempt once it is in the NRE account.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is FCNR deposit interest taxable in India?
entries.a: No, while you are a non-resident or RNOR for income tax. An FCNR(B) deposit is held in foreign currency for one to five years, and principal and interest are repatriable. The exemption ends once you become resident and ordinarily resident. Check whether your country of residence taxes it.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI maintain a savings account in India after moving abroad?
entries.a: Not as a resident account. Once you are a person resident outside India under FEMA, an existing resident savings account should be redesignated as NRO. Tell your bank when you leave. You can then keep NRO for Indian income and NRE for foreign earnings.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI be taxed in two countries on the same income?
entries.a: Yes. India may tax income arising in India, and your country of residence may tax your worldwide income. A tax treaty decides which country can tax and how much, and the country of residence usually gives credit for tax paid in India.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI avoid double taxation?
entries.a: Pay the lower treaty rate in India where one applies, using a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 41. Then claim credit for the Indian tax in your country of residence, under its rules. Keep Form 26AS and TDS certificates as proof, as that country will usually ask for them.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement?
entries.a: It is a treaty between India and another country that allocates taxing rights on income such as interest, dividends, royalties, salary and capital gains. Under section 159 (formerly section 90), you can use the treaty or Indian law, whichever is more beneficial. India has treaties with many countries, including the UAE, USA, UK, Singapore and Canada.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI claim DTAA benefits in India?
entries.a: Get a Tax Residency Certificate from your country of residence and e-file Form 41 (formerly Form 10F) where needed. Give these to the bank or payer before TDS is deducted, and claim the relief in your return, which also reports the treaty article relied on. If TDS has already been deducted at the higher rate, recover the excess through the return.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is a Tax Residency Certificate?
entries.a: It is a certificate from the tax authority of your country of residence, confirming that you are resident there for a stated period. It is required to claim treaty relief in India. Obtain one for each year in which you claim relief, because Indian payers and the department will ask for it.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Is Form 10F mandatory for NRIs?
entries.a: Form 10F is now Form 41 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. It is needed with a Tax Residency Certificate when claiming treaty relief, if the certificate does not contain all the required details, and is filed online with your PAN. It is not needed if you are not claiming treaty relief.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI claim foreign tax credit in India?
entries.a: Generally no, because a non-resident is taxed in India only on Indian income. Foreign tax credit is mainly for residents taxed in India on foreign income, who claim it in Form 44 (formerly Form 67). An NRI usually claims credit for Indian tax in the country of residence.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What happens if tax has already been paid in the country of residence?
entries.a: It does not by itself reduce Indian tax on income arising in India. The treaty decides which country has the right to tax. If India has the right, your country of residence usually gives credit. If only the other country has the right, claim relief in your Indian return with a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 41.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How are mutual fund investments taxed for NRIs?
entries.a: For equity funds, gains held over 12 months are taxed at 12.5% above Rs 1.25 lakh a year, and gains held for less at 20%. Debt fund units bought from 1 April 2023 are generally taxed at slab rates. TDS is deducted on redemption, on the whole gain, so the Rs 1.25 lakh relief often has to be claimed through the return. Surcharge and cess apply.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is the capital gains tax on shares for NRIs?
entries.a: On listed shares sold on an exchange, gains held over 12 months are taxed at 12.5% above Rs 1.25 lakh a year, and gains held for 12 months or less at 20%. Unlisted shares are long-term after 24 months and taxed at 12.5%; if held for less, they are taxed at slab rates. Surcharge and cess apply. A tax treaty may change the result.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can NRIs invest in Indian mutual funds?
entries.a: Yes, using an NRE or NRO account, with KYC showing NRI status. Investments from NRE funds are generally repatriable. Some fund houses restrict investors from the USA and Canada because of reporting rules there, so check with the fund house first.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What is the tax on dividends received by NRIs?
entries.a: Dividends from Indian companies and mutual funds are taxable in India, generally at 20% plus surcharge and cess, and TDS is deducted at that rate. A lower treaty rate may apply if you give a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 41 to the company or registrar before payment.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Are NRI investments in Indian shares taxable?
entries.a: Holding shares is not taxed. Dividends and gains on sale are. Rates depend on the type of share and the holding period, and the route used to buy them matters for repatriation, so keep your broker and bank records.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI claim deductions under Section 80C?
entries.a: Yes, under the old regime only. An NRI can claim life insurance premiums, equity-linked savings schemes, children's tuition fees and home loan principal, formerly under section 80C. An NRI cannot open a new PPF account or buy NSC. Under the new regime, which is the default, these deductions are not available.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What are the tax implications of selling inherited shares?
entries.a: Receiving shares by inheritance is not taxed. When you sell, the previous owner's cost and holding period count, and the usual capital gains rates apply. Keep the transmission documents and the original purchase records. Without them, the gain is hard to support.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How are investments taxed when an NRI returns to India?
entries.a: Gains on Indian investments continue to be taxed under the usual rules. Your broker, fund houses and banks must be told of the change of status, and NRE-linked holdings moved to resident status. Foreign investments stay outside Indian tax while you are RNOR, and become taxable and reportable once you are resident and ordinarily resident. See returning to India.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: I am an NRI and have received an income tax notice in India. What should I do?
entries.a: Note the section, tax year and reply date, and check that it appears on the e-filing portal under Pending Actions. Update your overseas email and mobile there. Compare the items with your AIS, Form 26AS and records, then reply online by the date. If you need more time, ask for it before the date. Do not ignore it, as an order can be passed without your side.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI respond to an income tax notice from abroad?
entries.a: Reply through the e-Proceedings section of the e-filing portal, uploading your explanation and documents. A personal hearing, where available, can generally be held by video. Keep the acknowledgement. An authorised representative can also reply for you.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Why has the Income Tax Department issued a notice to an NRI?
entries.a: Common reasons include a property sale with no return filed, high-value transactions in AIS, interest or rent not reported, a wrong residential status, foreign remittances, and a claim for TDS or treaty relief not matching the records. Sometimes the notice arises from a wrong address or PAN entry, which also needs correcting.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI correct an income tax return?
entries.a: A revised return can be filed for FY 2025-26 up to 31 December 2026, or up to 31 March 2027 with a late fee. After that, an updated return is available within the time limit, with additional tax, but not to claim a refund or reduce tax. Mistakes apparent from the record can be corrected by rectification under section 287 (formerly section 154).
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What happens if TDS deducted from an NRI's income is not reflected in Form 26AS?
entries.a: Credit may be denied when the return is processed. Ask the deductor, such as the buyer, bank or tenant, to file or correct the TDS statement with your correct PAN. Keep the TDS certificate as evidence. Claim the credit once it appears, or file a response with the proof if a demand is raised.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI authorise a Chartered Accountant to represent them before the Income Tax Department?
entries.a: Yes. A chartered accountant can act as your authorised representative. You add the authorisation on the e-filing portal and give a written authority, and the representative then replies and attends on your behalf. You stay responsible for the facts given, so check replies before they go in.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: How can an NRI resolve an income tax refund issue?
entries.a: Check the refund status on the portal, and confirm that the bank account is pre-validated and that the return has been verified and processed. Respond to any adjustment notice for old demands. If it remains stuck, raise a grievance through the e-Nivaran facility, or with the Centralised Processing Centre, using the return's acknowledgement number.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: Can an NRI respond to income tax proceedings without travelling to India?
entries.a: Yes, in most cases. Assessments and appeals are largely handled online, with replies uploaded and hearings by video where allowed. Your authorised representative can act for you. Travel may be needed only in unusual matters, such as a summons or court proceedings.
entries.t: NRI tax questions: status, returns, property, banking and DTAA

entries.q: What are the major changes introduced by the Income-tax Act, 2025?
entries.a: The Act replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026. It uses simpler language, tables in place of long provisos, and fewer sections, and it replaces previous year and assessment year with tax year. TDS provisions are consolidated in section 393. It is mainly a rewrite rather than a change in tax policy, though later Finance Acts amend it.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: What is the difference between the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the Income-tax Act, 2025?
entries.a: The 1961 Act governs tax years beginning before 1 April 2026, and the 2025 Act governs later ones. The structure, section numbers, terms and forms differ, but most concepts, such as heads of income, residence and capital gains, carry over. Check the old and new text together on any point that matters, because a changed word can change the result.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: How are the provisions of the old Act mapped to the new Act?
entries.a: The Income Tax Department has published correlation tables. Some examples: section 139 is now section 263, section 148 is section 280, section 154 is section 287, section 90 is section 159, section 54 is section 82, and sections 194C, 194J and others are in section 393(1). Section 6 on residence keeps its number. Use the official tables rather than guessing, as one old section can split into several.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: What is the concept of Tax Year under the new Act?
entries.a: A tax year is the 12 months from 1 April to 31 March in which the income is earned. For a new business or a new source of income, it begins on the date of set-up or when the source arises, and ends on the next 31 March. The tax is assessed and the return is filed by reference to that same year.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: How are Assessment Year and Previous Year replaced?
entries.a: Both are replaced by the single term tax year. Income of 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 is income of tax year 2026-27. Under the old Act, the same period would have been previous year 2026-27 and assessment year 2027-28. Earlier years keep the old terms.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: Which Act applies to income earned up to 31 March 2026?
entries.a: The Income-tax Act, 1961, through the savings provision in section 536 of the 2025 Act. So the return for FY 2025-26, its assessment, and any penalty or appeal for that year follow the 1961 Act, even though they take place after 1 April 2026.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: How are pending assessments and appeals dealt with under the new Act?
entries.a: CBDT's FAQs issued on 6 July 2026 say proceedings for tax years before 1 April 2026 continue under the 1961 Act, including those started later for such years. Assessments for tax year 2026-27 onwards fall under the 2025 Act. Appeals on earlier years should be approached in the same way, and the notice or order should show the provision being used.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: What happens to existing registrations, approvals and exemptions?
entries.a: They generally continue. CBDT's FAQs say section 12AB and 80G registrations already granted remain valid and protected under section 536. Applications filed by 31 March 2026 and still pending may be disposed of under the old Act or, for relief from tax year 2026-27, treated as filed under the new one. Check the expiry date on each approval, as renewal is still needed.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: What are the changes in Income-tax Rules and prescribed forms?
entries.a: The Income-tax Rules, 2026 apply from 1 April 2026, with renumbered forms. Examples: Form 16 is now 130, Form 16A is 131, Form 26Q is 140, Form 24Q is 138, Form 13 is 128, Forms 15G and 15H are 121, and Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD are 26. Old forms continue for old periods, so the form depends on the year and not the date of filing.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: How are tax payments and advance tax obligations handled during the transition?
entries.a: Advance tax for FY 2025-26, including the March 2026 instalment, fell under the 1961 Act. Advance tax for tax year 2026-27 falls under the 2025 Act, with the instalment dates unchanged: 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March. When paying online, select the correct year and section, as a wrong selection needs correction later.
entries.t: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed and how the transition works

entries.q: What are the applicable TDS provisions for professional fees?
entries.a: Under section 393(1) (formerly section 194J), tax is deducted at 10% where fees exceed Rs 50,000 in the year. The rate is 2% for technical services other than professional services, call centres and certain royalties. An individual or HUF not liable to tax audit may be outside this provision, unless a separate one applies.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: When is TDS applicable on payments to contractors?
entries.a: Where a single payment exceeds Rs 30,000, or total payments in the year exceed Rs 1 lakh (formerly section 194C). The rate is 1% for an individual or HUF contractor and 2% for others, on work including manpower supply, as clarified from 2026. Transporters with up to 10 goods carriages who give PAN and a declaration are excluded. Payments for personal purposes by individuals are also excluded.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What are the TDS provisions applicable to commission and brokerage?
entries.a: Tax is deducted at 2% where commission or brokerage exceeds Rs 20,000 in the year (formerly section 194H). An individual or HUF not liable to tax audit is generally not required to deduct under this head, unless the separate provision for large payments applies. Insurance commission has its own provision.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What is the TDS treatment of rent paid by individuals and businesses?
entries.a: Businesses deduct 10% on land, buildings and furniture, and 2% on plant and machinery, where rent exceeds Rs 50,000 a month (formerly section 194-I). An individual or HUF not under audit deducts 2% where rent exceeds Rs 50,000 a month, using PAN-based Form 141 without a TAN (formerly section 194-IB). Rent to a non-resident landlord falls under section 393(2) with no such limit.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What are the TDS implications on purchase of immovable property?
entries.a: A buyer from a resident deducts 1% where the consideration is Rs 50 lakh or more, excluding agricultural land (formerly section 194-IA). The tax is deposited with Form 141 within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction, and no TAN is needed. If stamp duty value is higher, the rate applies on that value. Buying from a non-resident is different: see NRI property TDS.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What are the TDS provisions for purchase of goods?
entries.a: A buyer whose turnover exceeded Rs 10 crore in the preceding year deducts 0.1% on purchases from a resident seller above Rs 50 lakh in the year, on the excess over Rs 50 lakh (formerly section 194Q). If the seller has no PAN, the rate is 5%. Sale of goods TCS under the old section 206C(1H) ended from 1 April 2025.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What are the consequences of non-deduction or short deduction of TDS?
entries.a: The payer can be treated as an assessee in default for the tax not deducted, with interest of 1% a month or part of a month. A business also loses 30% of a payment to a resident as a deduction, and all of a payment to a non-resident, until the tax is paid. Penalty and prosecution can apply in serious cases. Relief is available if the payee has included the income and paid tax, with an accountant's certificate.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: Can a deductor claim relief for TDS deposited late?
entries.a: Interest of 1.5% a month or part of a month must still be paid, and is not generally waived. Business expenses disallowed for late deposit are allowed if the tax is paid by the return due date, or otherwise in the year of payment. A long delay can lead to prosecution, so pay the tax and interest as soon as the default is found.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What is the procedure for correction of TDS returns?
entries.a: Download the consolidated file from TRACES, correct PAN, challan or amount details with the return preparation utility, validate, and upload it. Quarters to March 2026 use the old forms, and later quarters use the new ones. One source says correction is now limited to two years from the end of the year in which the original statement was due, so check the portal early.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: How should excess TDS or TCS be adjusted or refunded?
entries.a: A payee claims excess tax as a refund in the income tax return. A deductor who deposited too much can use the unconsumed balance against later liabilities through a correction statement, or apply for a refund through TRACES where it was paid by mistake. The money cannot be taken back once it has been credited to the payee.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What are the implications of incorrect PAN or non-furnishing of PAN?
entries.a: Tax is generally deducted at 20%, or the applicable rate if higher, and 5% in some cases such as purchase of goods. An inoperative PAN is treated in the same way. The payee can lose credit too, because credit follows Form 26AS. The separate higher rate for non-filers under the old sections 206AB and 206CCA has been removed.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What are the consequences of late filing of TDS statements?
entries.a: A late fee of Rs 200 a day applies, capped at the tax in the statement, and it must be paid before the statement is filed. A penalty can also apply for late or incorrect statements. Statements are due on 31 July, 31 October, 31 January and 31 May, and certificates depend on them, so delay also affects payees.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: How are TDS provisions applied to payments credited before 1 April 2026 but paid afterwards?
entries.a: The Act is decided by the earlier of credit or payment. If the amount was credited on or before 31 March 2026, the 1961 Act applies, with the old section codes, forms and certificates, even if it was paid later. New forms apply only where the earlier event is on or after 1 April 2026. Do not deduct twice on one amount.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: Which forms are used for quarterly TDS and TCS statements from tax year 2026-27?
entries.a: For quarters from April 2026, quarterly statements are filed in Form 138 for TDS on salary (formerly Form 24Q), Form 140 for TDS on other payments to residents (formerly Form 26Q), Form 144 for payments to non-residents (formerly Form 27Q) and Form 143 for TCS (formerly Form 27EQ). Statements for quarters up to March 2026, including corrections, stay in the old forms. The due dates are 31 July, 31 October, 31 January and 31 May.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: What does “Has the statement been filed earlier for this quarter?” mean in a TDS return?
entries.a: The return preparation utility asks whether a regular statement for the same TAN, form and quarter has already been filed. For the first statement of that quarter, answer No. If a statement for the quarter was filed and accepted, a fresh regular statement is not the way to change it; download the consolidated file from TRACES and file a correction statement quoting the token number (provisional receipt number) of the original. A separate question asks whether a regular statement was filed for an earlier period; answer Yes and give that statement's token number if one was.
entries.t: TDS and TCS for tax year 2026-27: rates, defaults and corrections

entries.q: Who is required to file an Income-tax return?
entries.a: Companies and firms must file regardless of income or loss. Individuals, HUFs, AOPs and BOIs must file if income exceeds the basic exemption limit, which is Rs 4 lakh in the new regime and Rs 2.5 lakh in the old regime. Filing is also required for certain high-value spending and deposits, to carry forward business or capital losses, and for residents with foreign assets.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: Which ITR form is applicable to different categories of taxpayers?
entries.a: ITR-1 is for residents with simple salary, one house and other income, up to Rs 50 lakh. ITR-2 is for individuals and HUFs with no business income, including capital gains. ITR-3 is for business or professional income. ITR-4 is for presumptive income of residents. ITR-5 covers firms and LLPs, ITR-6 companies, and ITR-7 trusts and specified bodies.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: What is the difference between an original, belated, revised and updated return?
entries.a: An original return is filed by the due date. A belated return is filed after it, with a late fee. A revised return corrects an original or belated return. An updated return discloses omitted income later, with additional tax. For FY 2025-26, see the table on this page.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: Under what circumstances can an updated return be filed?
entries.a: To report income omitted or wrongly reported, including where no return was filed, within 48 months from the end of the following year. Tax, interest and additional tax of 25%, 50%, 60% or 70% must be paid first, depending on the delay. It is not allowed in some cases, such as after search. Since 2026 it can also follow a reassessment notice, at rates 10 percentage points higher.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: Can an updated return be filed to reduce tax liability or claim a refund?
entries.a: No. An updated return cannot reduce tax, or create or increase a refund. From 2026 it can reduce a reported loss. If you have overpaid tax, use a revised return within its time limit. After that, the only routes are narrow ones, such as an application for condonation of delay.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: What are the consequences of filing an incorrect ITR?
entries.a: The return may be adjusted at processing, or selected for scrutiny or a notice. Tax, interest and penalty can follow, generally 50% of the tax for under-reporting and 200% for misreporting. A knowingly false return can lead to prosecution. Correct the error early with a revised or updated return, as voluntary correction usually limits the cost.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: How can an assessee rectify an intimation under section 143(1)?
entries.a: Compare it with your return, AIS and Form 26AS. For a mistake apparent from the record, file an online rectification on the portal (section 287, formerly section 154). If your return had the error, revise it, if time allows, or rectify using the correct data. If it involves a real dispute, consider an appeal within 30 days. See a wrong demand.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: What is the procedure for claiming an Income-tax refund?
entries.a: Claim it in the return, and pre-validate a bank account linked to your PAN. Verify the return within 30 days. The refund is issued after processing, and you can track its status on the portal. Check any notice about adjustment against old demands, because that can hold up the refund.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: What are the provisions relating to interest on delayed refunds?
entries.a: Interest is generally 0.5% a month or part of a month. If the return was filed on time, it usually runs from 1 April after the year, and if filed late, from the filing date, up to the date of refund. No interest applies if the refund is under 10% of the tax payable, and any delay caused by the taxpayer is excluded.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: How should AIS and Form 26AS mismatches be reconciled?
entries.a: Download both, along with your bank, broker and TDS records. Match each item by payer, amount and date. Separate genuine income from duplicates and wrong entries, and report the correct figure in the return. Keep the working, as it is the basis for any later reply. See AIS and Form 26AS reconciliation.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: What is the procedure for correcting incorrect information in AIS?
entries.a: Log in to the AIS portal, choose the entry and give feedback, such as income belonging to another person, duplicate, or not fully correct. The information may then go to the source for confirmation. Feedback does not change Form 26AS or your TDS credit, so a wrong TDS entry must be corrected by the deductor.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: How are refunds adjusted against outstanding tax demands?
entries.a: The department can set a refund off against an outstanding demand, after giving you notice (formerly section 245). Reply online within the time given, usually 30 days: agree, disagree with reasons, or mention an appeal or stay. If the demand is wrong, say so with documents, otherwise the refund may be adjusted.
entries.t: Income tax returns and refunds: forms, dates and corrections

entries.q: What are the consequences of non-verification of an Income-tax return?
entries.a: A return not verified within 30 days of filing is treated as not filed. You may then lose the refund, or face a late fee and interest, and some losses cannot be carried forward. The date of verification can be treated as the date of filing if you are late. A request for condonation is possible where there is genuine cause.

entries.q: What are the tax implications under the old and new tax regimes?
entries.a: The new regime has lower slab rates and a Rs 60,000 rebate up to Rs 12 lakh of income, but allows few deductions. The old regime has higher rates, with deductions such as those formerly under sections 80C and 80D, HRA and home loan interest. The new regime applies unless you opt out. Special-rate income, such as capital gains on shares, is taxed the same way in both.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: When should an individual opt for the old tax regime instead of the new regime?
entries.a: When your deductions and exemptions are large enough to bring the old regime's tax below the new regime's. This usually needs a combination such as HRA, section 80C investments, health insurance and home loan interest. Work out both every year with your actual figures. You can try the regime calculator.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: What deductions are available under the new tax regime?
entries.a: The main ones are the Rs 75,000 standard deduction for salary and pension, the employer's NPS contribution up to 14% of basic and DA, a family pension deduction up to Rs 25,000, and the Agniveer Corpus Fund. Retirement exemptions, such as gratuity, also stay. Interest on a let-out property reduces its rent, but a loss cannot be set against other income.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: How is the tax rebate calculated for an individual taxpayer?
entries.a: A resident individual gets a rebate up to Rs 60,000 under the new regime if total income does not exceed Rs 12 lakh, and up to Rs 12,500 under the old regime if it does not exceed Rs 5 lakh. It reduces tax before cess (section 156, formerly section 87A). It does not apply against tax on income at special rates, such as gains on listed shares. Non-residents do not get it.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: How is marginal relief calculated?
entries.a: Under the new regime, if income is slightly above Rs 12 lakh, tax is limited to the amount by which income exceeds Rs 12 lakh. On Rs 12.10 lakh, slab tax is Rs 61,500, but you pay only Rs 10,000 plus cess. Marginal relief also applies at the surcharge levels of Rs 50 lakh and Rs 1 crore and above, so extra tax does not exceed the extra income.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of salary, bonus, incentives and perquisites?
entries.a: Salary is taxed when due or when paid, whichever is earlier. Bonus and incentives are taxed in the year of receipt or when they become due. Perquisites are valued under the rules: the Income-tax Rules, 2026 revised some values from 1 April 2026, including tax-free meals up to Rs 200. Check the current company car and other values with payroll, and the Form 130 issued (formerly Form 16).
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation?
entries.a: Employer PF up to 12% of salary is not taxed. Employer NPS is deductible up to 14% of basic and DA under the new regime, and 10% for private employees under the old. Employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation above Rs 7.5 lakh a year together are taxable, with the income on that excess. Interest on employee PF contributions above Rs 2.5 lakh a year is taxable too.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: How are leave encashment and gratuity taxed?
entries.a: Leave encashed during service is taxable. At retirement or resignation, government employees are fully exempt. Others are exempt up to the lowest of the actual amount, Rs 25 lakh over a lifetime, 10 months' average salary, and unused leave value. Government gratuity is fully exempt. Others are exempt up to Rs 20 lakh, subject to a formula based on salary and years of service.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: What are the tax implications of voluntary retirement compensation?
entries.a: Up to Rs 5 lakh is exempt, once in a lifetime, if the scheme meets the conditions in the rules, which include 10 years of service or age 40. The excess is taxed as salary. If you take this exemption, you cannot also claim arrears relief for the same amount. The exemption stays available under the new regime.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: Can an individual change the tax regime after filing the original return?
entries.a: A person without business income chooses in the return, and can generally change it in a revised return only up to the original due date. After that date, including in a belated return, the new regime applies. A person with business income needs Form 10-IEA or its current equivalent by the due date, and can return to the old regime only once. Check the position for your year before relying on this.
entries.t: Old and new tax regimes, and how salary is taxed

entries.q: How are short-term and long-term capital gains computed?
entries.a: Start with the sale price, deduct transfer costs, then cost of acquisition and improvement. Listed shares and equity funds are long-term after 12 months, and property and most unlisted assets after 24 months. Indexation is generally not available on current long-term sales, with one exception for resident owners of older land and buildings. Holding period runs from the date of acquisition.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What are the applicable capital gains tax rates?
entries.a: Listed equity shares and equity funds on which STT is paid: 20% short-term, and 12.5% long-term on gains above Rs 1.25 lakh a year. Other long-term assets: generally 12.5%. Other short-term assets: slab rates. Debt funds bought from 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates. Surcharge and 4% cess are added. See the table on this page.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of sale of residential property?
entries.a: Held over 24 months, the gain is long-term, taxed at 12.5% without indexation. A resident individual or HUF who bought before 23 July 2024 can choose 20% with indexation if that is lower. Held for less, it is added to income at slab rates. If stamp duty value exceeds the price by over 10%, the stamp duty value is generally used. The buyer may deduct 1% TDS.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What are the exemptions available under sections 54, 54F and 54EC?
entries.a: Section 82 (formerly 54): gain on a house, reinvested in a house in India. Section 86 (formerly 54F): sale of another long-term asset, with the net sale proceeds reinvested in a house. Both allow purchase one year before or two years after sale, or building within three years, capped at Rs 10 crore. Section 85 (formerly 54EC): up to Rs 50 lakh in specified bonds within six months, for land or buildings.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of compulsory acquisition of property?
entries.a: The gain is taxed in the year the compensation is first received, and any later enhanced compensation is taxed when received. Compensation for urban agricultural land, and acquisitions under the 2013 land acquisition law, can be exempt if conditions are met. Read the award and the law it is under before filing, as the treatment depends on these.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: How is the cost of acquisition determined for inherited property?
entries.a: Cost is what the previous owner paid, and the previous owner's holding period counts. For property acquired before 1 April 2001, you can use its fair market value on that date, but not above stamp duty value for land and buildings. Keep the will or succession document, the old deed and any valuation report.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: How are capital gains calculated on sale of unlisted shares?
entries.a: Sale price less cost and transfer costs. Held over 24 months, the gain is long-term, taxed at 12.5%; otherwise, it is taxed at slab rates. If the price is below fair market value under the rules, that value can be taken as the sale price. Buyers paying below fair market value may also be taxed. Keep a valuation report.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of sale of listed equity shares?
entries.a: Where STT is paid: gains held for 12 months or less are taxed at 20%. Longer-held gains are taxed at 12.5% above Rs 1.25 lakh a year in total. Shares bought before 1 February 2018 can use the 31 January 2018 price as cost, within limits. Report the sale in the capital gains schedule, and match it with AIS.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: How are capital gains on mutual funds calculated?
entries.a: Sale value less purchase cost, unit by unit, with the earliest units treated as sold first. Equity funds follow the rates for listed shares. Debt funds bought from 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates however long they are held. Other funds depend on the type of fund and holding period. Use the capital gains statement from the fund or registrar.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of bonus shares and rights shares?
entries.a: Bonus shares are not taxed on receipt. On sale, cost is generally nil and the holding period runs from allotment, except for the 31 January 2018 rule on older bonus shares. Rights shares have a cost equal to the amount paid. If you sell the right itself, the gain is short-term, with nil cost for the original holder.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: How are capital gains calculated on transfer of depreciable assets?
entries.a: Depreciable assets are in a block. Sale proceeds reduce the block, and a gain arises only if proceeds exceed the block value, or the block ceases to exist. The gain is treated as short-term, whatever the holding period. The 12.5% rate may still apply in some cases, as courts have held for long-held assets, so check this if the amount is material.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What is the tax treatment of gifts of immovable property and shares?
entries.a: The giver has no capital gains on a gift. A receiver who is a relative pays no tax. A non-relative pays tax if property stamp duty value exceeds Rs 50,000, or if shares and other movable property exceed Rs 50,000 in total in the year at fair market value. On later sale, the receiver uses the previous owner's cost and holding period. See gifts.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What are the tax implications of joint development agreements?
entries.a: For an individual or HUF landowner with a registered agreement, the gain is taxed in the year the completion certificate is issued, not when the land is handed over. The value is the stamp duty value of the owner's share on that date, plus any cash. The developer deducts 10% TDS on cash paid. Sale of the share before the certificate, or an unregistered agreement, changes the result.
entries.t: Capital gains tax: rates, exemptions and common transactions

entries.q: What is the section 80-IAC tax holiday?
entries.a: It is a 100% deduction of profits from an eligible startup business, for any three consecutive years within the first ten years from incorporation. For tax year 2026-27 onwards, the provision is section 140 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, on broadly the same conditions. For FY 2025-26 and earlier, section 80-IAC of the 1961 Act applies.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: Who is eligible for the section 80-IAC deduction?
entries.a: A private limited company or LLP, incorporated from 1 April 2016 and before 1 April 2030, with DPIIT recognition and a certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board. Turnover must not exceed Rs 100 crore in the year of claim. Partnership firms, one-person companies and proprietorships cannot claim it, and the business must not be formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing one.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: Is DPIIT recognition enough to claim 80-IAC?
entries.a: No. DPIIT recognition is free and quick, and it is required first, but it does not give the deduction. You also need a separate certificate of eligibility from the Inter-Ministerial Board, which reviews innovation, scalability, market potential and employment. Fewer startups clear this stage, so a well-supported application matters.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: What is the turnover limit for 80-IAC after the 2026 DPIIT notification?
entries.a: The DPIIT notification dated 4 February 2026 raised the recognition limit to Rs 200 crore, and Rs 300 crore for deep tech startups. Commentators say the 80-IAC limit stays at Rs 100 crore in the year of claim, as no change has been reported. So a startup can be recognised and still not qualify for the deduction in a year with higher turnover.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: How do I apply to the Inter-Ministerial Board for 80-IAC?
entries.a: Apply online through the Startup India portal after DPIIT recognition. Set out the product or process, what is innovative, your business model and how it scales, supported by financial statements and any patents or other evidence. One source reports review within about 120 days of a complete application. Check the current portal checklist before filing.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: Which three years should a startup choose for 80-IAC?
entries.a: Generally the three consecutive years with the highest expected profits, within the ten-year window and while turnover is under the limit. Starting in a loss year wastes part of the benefit. Project profits, turnover and MAT before choosing. Once started, the years run consecutively.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: Does MAT apply to a startup claiming 80-IAC?
entries.a: Yes, for a company that is under the normal regime: Minimum Alternate Tax on book profits can still apply in the holiday years, and generally gives a credit under the rules. LLPs have their own alternate minimum tax rules. Budget 2026 changed parts of the MAT regime, so work out the current position before relying on this benefit.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: Can a company claim 80-IAC and the 22% concessional tax rate?
entries.a: Generally not. A company opting for the concessional rate formerly in section 115BAA gives up most Chapter VI-A deductions, including this one. Compare both for your expected profits and MAT position. A company that does not expect taxable profits in the window may find the concessional route simpler.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: What documents and filings are needed to claim 80-IAC?
entries.a: Keep the DPIIT recognition, Inter-Ministerial Board certificate, audited accounts, the prescribed audit report, and a working that separates profit from the eligible business. Claim the deduction in a return filed by the due date, because a late return generally loses it. Keep a yearly schedule of turnover against the Rs 100 crore limit.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: What is the difference between 80-IAC, the angel tax and carry forward of losses for startups?
entries.a: 80-IAC is a deduction on profits. Angel tax on share premium, formerly section 56(2)(viib), was abolished from FY 2024-25, so it no longer needs an exemption for new issues. Separately, an eligible startup can carry forward losses despite a change in shareholding, if conditions are met. Each has its own tests, so check them separately.
entries.t: Section 80-IAC: the startup tax holiday, now section 140

entries.q: How many days can an NRI stay in India without becoming resident?
entries.a: For most visiting Indian citizens and persons of Indian origin whose Indian income is ₹15 lakh or less, the limit is under 182 days in the tax year. If Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh, staying 120 days or more makes them resident if they also spent 365 days or more in India over the preceding four years.

entries.q: What is the 120-day rule for NRIs?
entries.a: It applies to Indian citizens and persons of Indian origin visiting India whose Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh. They become resident if they are in India for 120 days or more in the tax year and 365 days or more in the four preceding years. Anyone who is resident only because of this rule is treated as RNOR.

entries.q: Who is a deemed resident of India?
entries.a: An Indian citizen whose Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh and who is not liable to tax in any other country because of domicile or residence is deemed resident in India, whatever the number of days. A deemed resident is treated as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident.

entries.q: What is RNOR status and how long does it last?
entries.a: RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident) applies to a resident who was non-resident in nine of the ten preceding years, or was in India for 729 days or less in the seven preceding years. Foreign income, other than from a business controlled or profession set up in India, is not taxed in India in RNOR years. For someone returning after about ten years abroad, it usually lasts one to three years.

entries.q: Is residential status for income tax the same as under FEMA?
entries.a: No. Income tax status is based on days of stay in the tax year. FEMA status depends on the purpose and intention of the stay, and it governs bank accounts and investments. Both should be checked, as they decide different things.

entries.q: How are days in India counted for residential status?
entries.a: Days are counted from passport stamps or travel records for the tax year, 1 April to 31 March. The day of arrival and the day of departure are usually both counted as days in India, so a careful count is needed when you are close to a threshold.

entries.q: Does citizenship or passport decide residential status?
entries.a: No. Residential status depends on days in India, not on citizenship or passport. Citizenship matters only for the exceptions: the relaxed 182-day and 120-day rules apply to Indian citizens and persons of Indian origin, and deemed residency applies only to Indian citizens.

entries.q: What changes in my return when my status changes?
entries.a: A non-resident reports only Indian income. A resident and ordinarily resident reports worldwide income and must disclose foreign assets and foreign income. An RNOR reports Indian income and foreign income from a business or profession controlled in India. The return form, the schedules and the availability of treaty relief follow from the status.

entries.q: How much TDS should a buyer deduct when buying property from an NRI?
entries.a: The buyer deducts tax at the rate on the seller's capital gain, on the full price: 12.5% for property held over 24 months, or usually 30% if held for 24 months or less, plus surcharge (10% above ₹50 lakh, 15% above ₹1 crore) and 4% cess. On a long-term sale above ₹1 crore this is about 14.95% of the price, unless the seller has a lower deduction certificate.

entries.q: Is TDS on an NRI property sale deducted on the full price or only on the gain?
entries.a: On the full price. That is why TDS is often far higher than the actual tax. The seller can limit it to the tax on the gain by obtaining a lower deduction certificate in Form 128 before the sale.

entries.q: How can an NRI reduce TDS on a property sale?
entries.a: By applying on the TRACES portal for a lower deduction certificate in Form 128 (formerly Form 13), with the purchase deed, sale agreement, computation of the gain and any planned exemption. The buyer then deducts at the rate in the certificate. Apply as soon as the sale terms are agreed, because the certificate takes time to issue.

entries.q: Does the buyer need a TAN to deduct TDS from an NRI seller?
entries.a: From 1 October 2026, a buyer who is a resident individual or HUF can deduct and deposit this TDS using a PAN-based challan-cum-statement, without a TAN. Companies and firms buying from an NRI still need a TAN.

entries.q: How does an NRI get back excess TDS on a property sale?
entries.a: By filing an Indian income tax return for the tax year of the sale, reporting the gain, claiming the TDS credit and any exemption. The excess is refunded after the return is processed.

entries.q: Can an NRI save capital gains tax by reinvesting the sale proceeds?
entries.a: Yes. A long-term gain can be exempt if reinvested in a residential house in India within the prescribed period, subject to the overall cap, or if up to ₹50 lakh is invested in specified bonds within six months of the sale. Include the planned exemption in the lower deduction application.

entries.q: How can an NRI send property sale proceeds abroad?
entries.a: Proceeds credited to an NRO account can be remitted up to USD 1 million a financial year. The bank will ask for Form 145 (formerly Form 15CA) and, above the specified limits, a chartered accountant's certificate in Form 146 (formerly Form 15CB).

entries.q: Is TDS on the sale of a flat by an NRI different from a resident seller?
entries.a: Yes. For a resident seller, TDS is 1% and only where the price is ₹50 lakh or more. For a non-resident seller there is no threshold, and TDS is at the capital gains rate on the full price, plus surcharge and cess.
